A top-notch game. The writing and immersion are great, and the gameplay with its blend of both various challenges and ways to approach is engaging. The best hacking game since Uplink.
Good stuff! All keyboard interface is a great time.

Its gameplay doesn't have much to do with real-life hacking but it will make you feel like a hacker.
It's a collection of tactical minigames in which you move through abstract networks avoiding or eliminating obstacles and collecting resources. That's basically it. Comparing Midnight Protocol to Hacknet doesn't make much sense because the games are so different mechanically.

In addition to solid tactical puzzles that get more complex as the game progresses, there's a strong narrative wtih rpg elements - you choose to be a good or a bad guy and the story adapts. It would take at least 2 playthroughs to see all the content (one playtrough took me 21 hrs including all side missions in turn-based mode). Visuals are top notch, minimalistic and elegant. (However, I miss the ability to rotate the view like in Invisible Inc.). Soundtrack is beautiful and atmospheric and great to listen to on its own (though main theme is a bit too melancholic for this type of game). Level design is really solid and customizable loadout makes it fun to experiment with different approaches. My favourite level is Monarch&Reiter because it's multistage, complex and non-linear.

Make sure to try out real-time mode as it changes the gameplay completely, making it more exciting and similar to real-life hacking (and much less RNG reliant). It's ideal for a second playthrough once you're familiar with the commands and stuff. 

I'd recommend it to all tactical turn-based and hacking games fans and to keyboard ninjas. I really like the game setup and would love to see a sequel with improvements primarily in the story department - the game has huge potential.

the idea of the game is fairly innovative. however as an engineer i have some feature requests:
1. alt + backspace to delete a word at a time
2. alt + left/right arrow keys to move backward/forward one word

the above shortcuts is similar to that of linux terminal, i believe it will save us some time (you know, efficiency :) )

Yeah, I can see why less than 40% of players even finish the tutorial - too late now...

It's a nice idea, and possibly there are tactics that will improve your chances, but the very limited tutorials leave you with no idea what they might be, beyond blundering into traps or sneaking and sniffing while the counter inevitably goes up anyway...

I don't have time to spend dozens of hours on replays just to find out how best to beat the game - there's a little bit of storyline to keep you interested, but not much so far.
reviews.developer_response: The fact that only 40% of the players show to have finished the tutorial is easily explained by the fact that the achievements got added later as an update. The initial players are simply not included in the count.

reviews.review:
[h1] You are chaos embodied. [/h1]
Unhinged. Untested. Unstoppable. The keyboard is a natural extension of you. An arm, a tendril with which you tap into a vast, deep, unknowable ocean. 
And you believe the proper, nay, the only way to play chess is with a game clock. 
Act before you think. If you fail, try again. 
Run wild. Run blind. 

I do recommend that anyone interested in a keyboard/console based game give Midnight Protocol a shot. The RTS mode is an experience to be had. Besides, the demo is free, and I'm pretty sure you can already try that mode in there?

DISCLAIMER: This review is written for the RTS variant of gameplay. I have only played a bit past tutorial with its turn-based mode so there would be a bit of speculation on that portion of gameplay. 

I think the game truly had something unique, behind its "not recommended" way to play. It just feels so paradoxical: on one hand, I can't imagine them having developed this mode later, with so many of the game's elements seemingly originating from a more time-based perspective (for example, the money drain being continuous when you got fully-traced, or the final trace countdown in general). It also just feels impossible that someone would make a "hacking" game that doesn't reward lightning fast fingers and an innate familiarity with the console. On the other, so many of the "transplanted" features feel forced, imbalanced, as if the devs spent little effort trying to make the RTS mode actually enjoyable overall, among them the top culprits being oft-misleading card texts, or multiple challenges requiring interactions with the trace meter that is impossible to do in RTS, making them impossible to complete, or worse, Onion being a card that exists which completely trivializes the Trace Meter in RTS mode, and Hive being completely nuts that there's next to no reason to use any other breaker except for a select few situations. Perchance. 

I don't think any other game quite captures that chaotic energy as well as Midnight Protocol did for its first few missions. The scramble to get objectives done, timing drains just in time to avoid getting hit by its cooldown, juggling sniffers and dashing back and forth to sniff the next connection on an ice-ridden network... 
Quite unfortunately, the game trying to make itself a turn-based thing really runs at odds with its hacker-esque aesthetic. So many opportunities lost just to make it a middling strategy game with a mediocre story. That decision may have come from a genuine place of good intentions, perhaps to make it accessible to those not well-versed with a keyboard, or those who would much prefer the more methodical approach. Without a timer breathing down your neck, demanding you to act now, I don't think the Poison debuffs, or being backed into a corner by various bosses, would feel nearly as intense. The first time I ran through the first Wire Trial was most certainly heart-attack inducing. I ran blind. I ran wild. And miserable was my failure. Perchance. 

I don't know where this game belongs. It looks, feels and plays extremely polished and smooth, yet its mechanics, its progression/difficulty curve, and its -- quite frankly -- odd karma system adds very little to gameplay or story. It's as if a master of design did the moment-to-moment gameplay, a professional artist did the paintjob, then a monkey did everything in between. Perchance.

This game is very fun and *beautiful*.

It's a turn-based strategy with hand-crafted levels, and each new level is somehow interesting. The main story levels are the best but the even each new side level has a unique network composition or different hints or obstacles or even new gameplay elements, and together this makes it so that you're always looking forward to what you will see in the next level. The best experience is perhaps the level where you're chatting with your friend as you go, navigating a building and opening doors for her.

Another cool thing is that the game is beautiful. It has almost no art (some enemy defenses have pretty 3D models, but they're rare) but the interface shines. It has good fonts, crisp text rendering, sharp lines, no choppiness and is very responsive. Curiously, I find these things very important in text-based games and RPGs.

[b]TL;DR: If you're looking for something similar to HackNet, this is right up your street[/b]

Midnight Protocol is a hacking game along the veins of HackNet, although with several key differences.

The core gameplay loop has you preparing a set of programs and eventually hardware to infiltrate a network to do some fun hackerman deeds before the network traces your location and shuts you down. The programs and hardware you can equip get more varied, and the situations you find yourself in getting more and more complex as you inevitably build a rep for yourself in cyberspace. However, most players may find that a lot of situations can be solved with just a few programs.

Fans of the genre will have a lot to like about the game, and there are some unique mechanics that help differentiate it from other games, such as the main fact that the game has absolutely no mouse control whatsoever; every action you perform in-game is done solely through the use of the keyboard. This could be a little bit of a turn-off for some, but for others it'll no doubt add to the atmosphere.

One key criticism I can make about the game is that the game is sparse with details of a mission before you go into it for little reason. Other than a basic glance at the potential number of ICE on the network, presence of a SysOp, or required programs, your network scanner doesn't give much information, which would be fine if the game didn't have a command that let you just reset the mission the moment you begin.

All in all, this game can give you a good few hours of gameplay, and honestly I think more people need to play it. It's criminal that a game like this has gone so overlooked for so long.

[b]Love[/b] the game concept and everything about this, Requires some YnJhaW4gY2VsbHMgYW5kIGNvbWl0bWVudA== to go with it, so its not for anVzdCBhbnkgZ2FtZXIgb3V0IHRoZXJl I can say. 

[spoiler]https://youtu.be/zGSjPPySCD0[/spoiler]

The reality is this game has a good atmosphere and a great gimmick, the thing is it lost me the moment it started putting turn caps on the levels. The fun for me was to work around the trace meter, and to use tools to try and stay in and get as much as I could done, by switching it form an avoid game to a rush game, it was single-handidlyruined for me. If you have a similar mindset, i highly do not recommend this game.

An interesting concept. With all the interesting programs you can add to your deck, this should have been a solid turn-based strategy/puzzle game, but it's so restrictive and RNG-based from the start that it can easily turn into a "try, die, repeat until you get lucky" experience. After my sixth time restarting a single mission because of bad luck rather than lack of skill (getting a trace+ three times in a row despite having cloak at 75%, SysOps making a beeline for me at exactly the wrong moment, etc.), I realized I wasn't having fun anymore, so I turned it off and sorted it into my "not worth it" pile.

It's a shame, because there was a lot of potential to love here and it would have been right up my alley if the RNG was a little more forgiving.

EDIT: Devs have pointed out that there ARE difficulty settings. It took me a bit to find them, but they do exist, so I've edited the review to reflect that and to add examples for the bad luck I had.
reviews.developer_response:
The game offers exactly what you are asking for. There's options to tweak the difficulty to your liking.

Yes there's RNG elements but skill should prevail at all times. Winning a mission is not just a matter of luck.

reviews.review:
[h1]Midnight Protocol[/h1]

Interesting game, a wonderful time killer and definitely a hidden gem. I really wonder why more people aren't playing it. The game mixes hacking, puzzles, and storytelling into one fun little experience. It's nothing new, the story is just above average and there are a few flaws. And if you've played games like Uplink, Hacknet, Nite Team 4, or even the hacking part of the new Shadowrun games, you'll be familiar with most parts of the gameplay. But overall I have no hesitation in recommending the game at full price and definitely on sale.

[b]Postive:[/b]

1.) Immersion and atmosphere are top notch. The beginning is a bit rough, boring and repetitive, but it picks up the pace pretty quickly and doesn't slow down until the end. After the tutorial and the first few standard missions you can't and don't want to stop. Just "one" more mission and hours later, after some really intense battles and boss fights, you start to see the full potential of the game.

2.) Some missions and side missions are the real deal. I've had some of the most intense moments in recent memory, taking on other hackers or "bosses" in some highly dynamic puzzle battles. And not even in real time, just by typing commands into my keyboard. This is a great achievement by the developers. And some of the side missions are really well written.

3.) The soundtrack is great and a wonderful addition to the immersion and intensity during most missions.

4.) Graphics and user interface are minimalistic but quite polished. There is nothing to complain about.  didn't notice any bugs or crashes either.

[b]Neutral:[/b]

1.) The story could be a lot better. It's your well-known sci-fi/cyper story that you've heard, read, or seen many times. Maybe it would be ok if it was your first cyber/hacking game, but a little creativity here and the game would be a real masterpiece.

2.) The gameplay is strange at first. There doesn't seem to be much depth. But once you get used to the keyboard-only mechanics and get more and more programs and hardware to work with, the possibilities and depth get pretty good. You can build your deck based on your playstyle, but there are always some limitations on what programs you should bring. And some are just better than others. It's still good, but that's definitely a point where the game could be better. And that RNG can really mess thing up. 

[b]Cons:[/b]

1.) There is no manual saving. Yes, I understand it. It "adds" to the immersion or something like that. But in a game where you can take different paths and make certain decisions, I think a save function is an absolute must. Even more so when you have to play and answer certain side missions perfectly in order to see everything the game has to offer. And it's not so clear what to answer or what to do to advance the side story and get the next mission. I got pretty pissed when I read about things I missed while being very careful to avoid doing just that. But one wrong answer, or move and that's it. Better luck next time. I don't like this decision at all.

[b]Conclusion:[/b]

I don't know the full story behind the game and the devs, but only 131 reviews for a great title like this is just sad. It's about 25-30 hours of gameplay, fun, and intensity. It's a solid piece of work with a lot of commitment put into it and well worth the price and I hope more people find out about this hidden gem. If you like hacking/puzzle games or want to get into it, don't be shy. Try it out and if you like it, spread the word. Midnight Protocol deserves a good community as so far there are no achievement guides, walktroughts or tips for specific missions, deck/hardware discussions and the like.
Not worth it.

Midnight Protocol is a great way to relax if you want to get away from realism and just enjoy the style.
If I wanted realism, I'd go to HackTheBox or TryHackMe and actually mess around with real-world stuff.  But if I want enough of an abstraction of the activity of hacking, Midnight Protocol gives me that.
One drawback is that I find the soundtrack to be a bit dour, but it's really a small criticism.  It's a great soundtrack, I just think that other hacking games have a more "upbeat" feel to them, and it would be the perfect complement.  There's not enough energy and tension in the music, but this is a really forgivable shortcoming.
I also enjoy the classic names given to the hacking tools, it gives it a really "gamey" feel that reminds me of the card game "Android: Netrunner".  I'm not here for deep technical stuff, I just want enough there to remind me of hacking without it actually being hacking.  If my hacking tool is an actual flurry of swords breaking down an actual wall, that's fine with me.
If you want realism, get a subscription or a free account on TryHackMe or HackTheBox.  But if you want a nice little hacking game that's pretty fun that gives you plenty of strategic moments, play this game.

Let me start off by saying that this game is way better than Uplink. (Despite being somewhat inspired by it)

Midnight Protocol is a turn-based strategy game with some RPG elements. The game is 100% played on your keyboard and you type the commands that you want to perform while moving around a board. Commands range from offensive or stealth, with a multitude of types to choose from and while navigating the board, you are destroying/avoiding antivirus programs called ICE as well as security system admins called Sys ops. While it might not sound like much at first,  the gameplay is a solid, intense and addictive experience.

The story and characters in Midnight Protocol are enthralling, and kept me constantly guessing as to what was going to happen next. To be brief, you are a reputable hacker named DATA taking on jobs for people from all walks of life. Your jobs range from hacking into banks, planting evidence, and deleting evidence of infidelity off of some couples' iCloud to prevent some idiot's divorce. (No, seriously.) 

One thing that this game handles very well, in my opinion, is choice. In almost every mission, you are given a choice that affects your moral standing in the game' s world. The game measures your choices and you have 3 meters: White hat (Good), Black hat (Bad), Gray hat (Morally grey). A nice touch considering that hackers in this world (as well as somewhat in our own) are considered to be modern day outlaws. A good chunk of your choices are meaningful for the ending, and almost none are easy which I think is where this game really shines.

To get into negatives, there is a warning when you open the game that tells you that the game is controlled solely through the keyboard. That's completely understandable the first time you launch the game, but not every time. There’s also no way to turn this off for some reason to my knowledge and it became pretty annoying after launching the game for the first time. Another negative I wanted to mention is that there is a MAJOR difficulty spike towards the end of the game. Having things get harder towards the end of a game makes absolute sense, but it felt like the game’s difficulty curve went from an incline to a straight up 90 degree angle. 

To conclude, I wanted to leave this great game a review seeing as how it doesn’t have enough of them and definitely deserves a bit more love.

4/5

I want to like this game, but there are some frustrating design flaws that detract from what should be a fun hacklite game. I kept running into the same issues time and again throughout the campaign, here are a couple of examples.

- There are some storylines that require you to play perfectly to proceed. Failure can lock you out from retrying, and many times the way forward is very obtuse. For example, in one mission you must stop an assassin from boarding a train. To unmask the assassin in the first place you must have played efficiently enough in previous missions, to have had enough spare time left to investigate several non-objective data nodes. Then you have to figure out that one of the terms in an email can be searched for on the In[T]ranet, and then recall information from over a dozen missions earlier. In this mission you must now disrupt the track to delay the train, without affecting any other tracks, which also means failure. First you have to be inquisitive enough (and have enough trace time to) investigate a non-objective data node and find out that the target train has been rescheduled from track C to Track B. Upon sabotaging track B you get an update showing that the objective to stop the assassin from boarding was successful! Mission complete right? Well apparently not. Disconnecting at this stage gives you a blank mission summary and prevents you from reattempting the mission. As much as I want to know what went wrong I'm not willing to start the game from the beginning to try and find out.

- The RNG can really mess you up. This one is pretty simple, you need to use a stealth program to avoid the trace bar filling up. Instead of being based on turns or measured progress, it's a % chance to increase every turn. This means that sometimes running restrictive heavy stealth can fail you several times in a row, or sometimes token measures will prevent a trace for many turns in a row. Some missions have very low trace bars, meaning a bit of bad RNG can cause you to fail. Running into (randomly placed) ICE also increases trace, and you are forced to either waste time scanning for it or run into it headlong. There are many other examples of RNG messing up your timing or causing undue grief.

- The game throws a lot of unexpected curveballs and suckerpunches at you. This is made worse by the fact that you can only carry (by default) 5 programs with you on each mission.  Sure the portscanner on the mission selection screen will generally give you broad sense of what you might be facing, but the specifics really do matter. What if you pick hive (an attack program that is very weak at the start of the mission but becomes more powerful as you infect more nodes) and a wall ICE spawns between the access node and the rest of the network? Suddenly you spend half the trace bar just breaking through the first obstacle, leaving no time for the mission objectives. There's also a poorly pre-informed boss battle where the boss ICE/AI may randomly destroy one of your software packages. Yes, you can hack a specific node to disable this attack, but RNG decided that he would use it immediately on me and remove my only breaker app (ie I'm now unarmed against a boss). The game really likes throwing these kinds of scenarios at you out of left field, and failure usually means you can't re-attempt the mission without starting a new game.

- The Morality Penalty. Simply put, blackhat actions reward you grossly while whitehat actions leave you starving for resources. In many cases the whitehat missions available have no payout or even ask you to spend credits on the mission itself. Some of the better attack programs are also locked behind blackhat rank, while whitehat will give you an extra defensive option or two (sitting still spamming defensive measures is not great, a lot of missions have timers).

All in all, many of these could have been alleviated if there wasn't such a reliance on RNG or bringing the perfect combination of apps. As it is, many missions feel more like a gamble than proper foresight or strategy.

Midnight Protocol is an all right game that feels like it's one step away from worth recommending in every department.

Mechanically, using only keyboard commands winds up being more of a hindrance than an asset. So much targeting and movement could be done easier and quicker if the player was just allowed to click. Everything is already set up into a nice modern-looking GUI with discrete locations to mouse over and select. You just can't do that, and have to type anyway. 

As for the puzzles and difficulty, there are a few interesting challenges over the course of the game, but for the most part you are handled powerful enough tools that you rarely have to think very hard. There's also a lot of downtime while enemy turns and animations slowly play out, which means that even if you know the next ten moves you'll want to make, actually executing them can be tedious.

Plot-wise, the game sets up a specific narrative and conflict you will eventually become embroiled in and resolve, but it's a little light on motivations for the player to actually get invested. The story feels like it mostly depends on a couple big surprise twists to do the legwork, but without grounding the player before and after them, it doesn't feel like enough to make a great story.

Maybe if there was an absolute banger OST, or the solutions to the puzzles could get really really crazy, that would be enough to push the game over the cusp of greatness. As presented though, it feels overall a bit underwhelming.

You know, I almost think that the Indiepocalypse was a good thing. Before, you could release a pretty mediocre, unpolished experience and you'd still sell a bunch of copies. Now devs are scrambling to have absolutely all elements of the game adjusted to perfection... and have only 116 reviews on Steam. So there's a bunch of sublime, absolutely excellent titles on Steam which nobody plays, and the dev's life is ruined. Ok, that's not very nice actually.

Midnight Protocol is one of those games. It manages to reproduce the *feeling* of hacking while making the gameplay incredibly engaging, and tells a gripping, morally challenging story about the future of the internet and the reality of hacktivism. Just beware: this game is played using keyboard only, by typing commands. No time pressure, tho.

To explain the gameplay a bit more: it's nothing like other hacking games like Uplink; in fact it's unlike anything, full stop. It's a tactical turn-based "network crawler" in which you constantly try to avoid getting traced while trying to complete the mission objective (usually activate some node, or steal money, or download a piece of data). 

You'll have to deal with firewalls (ICEs), SysOps, and the unrelenting trace protocol which ticks every turn. And you're never 100% safe from it; it will get you eventually. But if you rush too much, you might run into firewalls, or alert the SysOp to your presence. So it becomes a constantly changing game of resource and risk management.

And the stakes are high. There are some routine, insignificant missions, yes. But the majority ask interesting questions about morality of technology, ask you to consider your principles, and some are literally about someone's life and death... and perhaps even more. That, combined with the ever ticking trace protocol, drive the tension through the roof - your brain is always at 100% processing while playing this; never a dull moment.

Of course, you're given a set of tools to accomplish your goals. Your deck - programs you bring with you on a mission, as well as your hardware - passive bonuses. As you progress, you unlock new pieces, which often you also have to buy, and money's tight early on. And while the hardware gives you a clear advantage, the new programs aren't necessarily better; everything comes with a cost. And it's up to you to construct a deck which minimises the cost but maximises the advantage, all while keeping an eye on what is best for this particular mission.

Of particular note is the music in this game. It breaks seemingly all rules of sensible design by having essentially two tracks playing for the majority of the game. One for "normal" missions, and one for more important ones. In the latter, as the trace bar slowly but surely fills, the music is becoming more and more intense. This takes the already sky-high feeling of tension and launches it into the outer orbit.

To wrap things up, writing. It's way better than I thought it would be. The story is coherent, has constant twists and turns, keeps you in its grip, and makes excellent usage of the Chekhov's Gun. It's also unique because it's a hacking story that takes place in the EU in the 2060s - and it's a very believable representation. Your character resides in Budapest, but other European cities also make an appearance, such as Berlin with it's tech hub. 

If you're wondering why I only wrote good things, it's because I can't really think of anything bad. And my standards are high. If anything, I'm very displeased that the game has only 116 reviews at the time of writing, indicating it didn't sell very well; I'm hoping I convinced you to help fix that problem a little. Enjoy!

I have been playing this game for some time and I always liked how immersive the game is.
I was there when it got playtested on G.Round, I have made videos on the game and even streamed it.
And now I come with something new! 

I recently got a Steamdeck (256GB version), and I am currently testing out how well games work on the SteamDeck etc.
So the following points will be about Midnight on the StreamDeck!

[h1] The Immersion I talked about.. [/h1]
The immersion is a bit gone on the Steam Deck as it's only partially playable, as the game is fully playable with keyboard. For the Steam Deck that means that you have to press the Steam button + the X button at the same time to open the keyboard. The immersion of hacking was a bit gone and I grew more tired of constantly having to do the button combinations and then press a letter on the keyboard and continue, sometimes having to do the same action 4 times in a row just to start a mission. I felt more like a developer than hacker doing this.
After a while you do get used to it, but it takes away some of the joy.

[h1] The Good [/h1]
The graphics defintly do not go to waste on the SteamDeck, it's fun to carry a 'puzzle'like game as Midnight Protocol with you and being able to play it where you go, the performance worked very well and I didn't experience any lag on the Deck. wtf?

First of all, the decision to shoehorn a keyboard-only interface was disastrously misguided. They took a game that was basically designed for a GUI and replaced the GUI with an awkward CLI. 

You know what's faster than typing in "map", just to look up the names of relevant nodes (the names of non-adjacent nodes being of course hidden from view for some reason and it's not like they are organized in a logical grid either), and then typing "sniper [node1] [node2]"? A SINGLE CLICK. Having to constantly reassign slices in order to optimize is another major pain. Almost every action could be done faster with a mouse and you feel it with everything you do.

This is of course the exact opposite of why hackers use the terminal. They use it because it's faster and more powerful (or they have no other choice for interacting with a remote host). They don't use it in order to deliberately make things slower and dumber for themselves.

I guess if you don't have this in mind when you play the game, you might feel like a 1337 haxxor pwning distant networks with nothing but your keyboard. But if you do understand all of the above, you will likely feel like your time is being wasted with terrible UX design. 

If the puzzles weren't lame and/or the story was not a forgettable cyberpunk cliche, then maybe dealing with these UX issues would be worth it, but neither of that is true.

When people talk about the power of indie video games, they mean games like this one. A tight turn-based strategy game underpins a well-written story with a branching narrative and compelling characters. The overall length of the game at 20 hours was, for me, absolutely perfect. This is a rare game where I picked it up on a discount and find myself angry I didn't pay more for the experience.

The game itself is about you, a hacker returning from a year of incarceration with a need to know what sent you there. Along the way, you breech systems in a turn-based strategy game similar to Invisible, Inc. Whereas in that game you play physical agents, in this one you play a digital representation ripped straight out of cyberpunk fiction like Neuromancer. Customize your deck with new chips so you can slot more programs and be prepared for some visual surprises - while the game plays true to form with the genre, it manages to break expectations any time the game begins to feel stale.

My biggest complaints (and they are fairly minor) are around the customizations. I felt like the deck you have has just a few too few viable options or that some choices didn't really seem plausible. For instance, you have the expected upgrades, such as more "slices" to run more programs at once, or memory capacity to slot more programs into your deck, but you also have a bunch of upgrades which feel pretty pointless. I tried one that was supposed to give you more credits (trailing a crimson thread behind you and incentivizing exploring a network more deeply) but the core upgrades are so important, there's not room for fanciful choices such as these. That said, there are actually enough choices that I did have to rearrange both my hardware and software to overcome levels, and that felt like I was making smart choices.

I will have to find time for another play-through now that I have a better sense of the story, and so I can capture all the easter eggs buried in this passion project. I hope someday we get a Midnight Protocol 2 in the same universe, though perhaps with different characters. And to the creators, thank you for bringing this story to life.

[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (~9 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] is a simple turn-based strategy game with a hacking theme. You'll be able to explore nodes in a network and use programs to get data from them. The game offers multiple story branching, missions, and unlockables based on the path that you choose.

[b]Pros:[/b]
- Story branching depends on your choice in the mission
- 2 endings
- Those who don't like to read can still enjoy the game without doing so
- Various programs and hardware to use based on the mission and playstyle
- Difficulty can be changed anytime you want

[b]Cons:[/b]
- RNG-based, especially at the beginning of the game
- It can take a while to wait until the enemy finishes their turn
- Missions will be treated as finished if you exit the network
- Contrasting colors in some cutscenes (red on top of black/grey) can be problematic to some people

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you enjoy playing hacking games and don't mind playing one in a different genre, buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
The visuals are divided into two parts: your computer and the network interface. The computer interface is more simplified, giving a lot of space to the text with switchable tabs. As for the network, they are depicted with a lot of interconnected nodes that you can travel to. To be honest, they don't look like a network at all, but the programs' visuals help to give that impression.

[h3]Story[/h3]
Dialogues in [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] are mostly about missions that you will take. A lot of events will happen at the same time as the main plot, which will get you involved in various things. I liked that they usually don't stop after one mission - it feels as if I was involved and making progress. As for the main plot, I found them to be alright. The presentation looks cool with the sudden contract of color, although some parts are still in mystery. The closure also feels realistic with everything going by as normal. However, despite the multiple endings, I don't think they differ that much to warrant another playthrough.

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
As I said before, the game is a turn-based strategy, albeit simplified. You'll have a series of interconnected nodes where you can travel and spawn programs to help you with your objectives. The objectives are varied in each mission, but basically, you need to explore all nodes and take out every object of interest, whether it's by downloading a file or routing money to your account. Some ICEs will guard some nodes in between, forcing you to spawn another program to take them out. Moreover, you need to do these while avoiding being traced, which will be randomized per turn based on your stealth capabilities.

Stealth is the most problematic aspect of this game. You only have a 75% chance not to be recognized enemy for each turn, and that's by using all of your slices, which is the equivalent of your system memory in-game. However, you will eventually need to summon more programs to do other things, which will require more slices. You can always lower the assigned slices in your stealth program, but doing so will lower its capabilities, making it easier for you to be traced by the enemy. I had to restart a mission several times in the beginning whenever the RNG screw me up and traced me every turn. It was boring to replay the missions and do the same thing again, hoping that the outcome will be different. The gear upgrades that were given after you play some missions help to overcome this, but you still need to tough it out before you got to that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759479057

The early game is tough. Not only is the stealth mechanic isn't reliable, but the randomized enemies also can screw your run. You need to walk efficiently and not waste turns due to the RNG-based stealth, but enemies' locations are always hidden until you ran into them or used a sniffer program. Both options are not good either - the first option will increase your trace bar while the second one will eat 2 slices for 2 turns. It is easier to memorize enemies' locations before attempting your real run, but some enemies are placed randomly between more than one path. Again, this can be mitigated by purchasing upgrades after you reach a certain point.

The game gets better after you get enough upgrades. The RNG-based gameplay is still there, but it won't affect much to your experience. Moreover, numerous programs are available to help you build a deck that suits your playstyle. Since some missions are easier if you bring a certain program, you're bound to swap the programs from time to time.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2632524112

The reputation system can increase your difficulty. The game has a system that categorizes you into either white hat, grey hat, or black hat. This gives an impression that you can only choose one, although you can get as many reputations as you want in all categories. Some story-related missions might give a different reputation and outcome based on your action, but you never have to worry about anything apart from that. I refrained from taking anything that might increase my black hat reputation at first, which only penalize me from getting a benefit from that category and more money.

Money is limited at the early game. This might give issues to those who are trying to play the game purely as white hats since they are restricted from taking money from certain nodes. Moreover, those who quit the mission halfway will get penalized even more since the mission will be treated as completed without getting any reward. The game will give you a lot of money near the end of the game, but you won't need it at that point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2759480074

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
The in-game clock says that I finished the game at 15:50:34, although [i]Steam[/i] said that I finished it in 26.6h. I had to retry some levels a few times to get a perfect result, and since you need to go to the main menu to buy more gears at the store in missions, it can take a while to load your save, especially with the unskippable animations. I spent the rest of my playtime figuring out the last achievement, which can be made shorter if you know what to do.

As for the difficulty, it can be hard at the beginning due to the RNG, but you can always change the difficulty in the options. I didn't change it apart from one mission, which I deemed impossible to finish at the normal difficulty due to the time limit. The final boss might also pose a problem if you choose to go on a certain route, although it is still doable by using certain programs.

[b]Problems[/b]
Some text can be hard to see due to the font color. Also, the in-game display can hinder you from seeing some information, such as the node address and how many turns you have left.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]Midnight Protocol[/b] might be unpleasant to play at first due to the RNG, but it will soon be enjoyable once you have access to certain upgrades. My focus went to completing missions instead of the story, which is always unique in certain aspects. The game also offers more gameplay through the Workshop feature, although I soon got bored since I had to deal with the RNG again without my upgrades. Although I found some aspects to be lacking, I still could recommend [b]Midnight Protocol[/b] at a sale, provided that you are fine with the RNG-based gameplay.

reviews.review:
I started this game out of curiosity because of it's unique visual style and game mechanics, and I ended up spending a surprisingly large number of hours playing it.

One could call Midnight Protocol a [i]hacking simulator[/i]. In truth, it's a puzzle game that you drive with your own keyboard. You can equip different programs, which enable different moves, and different hardware components, which modify some of the game parameters. Some of the puzzles were genuinely challenging, though none of them was insurmountable.

While progressing through the level, you discover the game story and backdrop by reading email you get from other characters and intel you gather while playing missions. The game occasionally lets you send email to other character but you often only have to choose between a couple different options, which influence which direction some of the secondary story lines take.

The plot itself is quite engaging, with an unexpected plot twist roughly two thirds into the game. I did find it interesting enough to spend multiple nights playing until I got to the end.

I ran into a handful small bugs, none of which was insurmountable though. I had to restart a couple levels because the game was stuck when processing a new turn. The developers seem to have been quite active in the community and responsive to user feedback.

Overall, I'd recommend Midnight Protocol. It really does take inspiration from the Hollywood hacking aesthetic (in that, it does differ from games like Hacknet). However, it does that in a very measured way: the visual style and sound design add up to the atmosphere. The puzzle mechanics are quite novel, and I'd encourage you to give it a shot.

An enjoyable investigative puzzle game, Midnight Protocol has good writing, reinforced by clever changes in the UI and the visual respresentation of dataspace with every level. The game succeeds in creating the appropriate mood when it needs to, with music that alters alongside the tension, or meta elements involving a desktop crash or UI corruption. Some of the puzzles require innovative thinking, or a re-examination of what is at your disposal, which makes it rewarding to find a solution.

The strategic part comes through the deck and hardware customisation, which is well-tied into the story and gameplay. Optional challenges for extra credits encourage change; combined with mission-required programs and the natural slot limit, it encourages you to think and change your plan as required. I found the 'rollback' command, allowing the player to retry the mission with a different loadout, to be an essential part of adapting an approach, as the tactics to complete an actual level is tied heavily into your loadout choices. No prior knowledge of programming is required to play, and the game provides in-level help for any command the player needs.

The percentage chance for trace progression, which leads to a level's failure condition, is something that might appear frustrating if the player has few options (such as near the beginning of the game with limited programs available), but no level is impossible, and as a turn-based game with unlimited retries, there is plenty of time to think and plan, which makes the eventual success more satisfying.

At face value I was uncertain, but after twenty-eight hours of playtime and playing nothing else until I finished it, I am certain that Midnight Protocol is a good game that could be worth your attention.

I got this from Humble Bundle's Humble Choice January 2022. I've played Hacknet (another great hacking game) and thought this would be similar based off the screenshots. The only similarities is that they are both hacking themed, and you could type commands.

[h1] Playthrough [/h1]
Midnight Protocol took me almost 30hours to 100%, which was done in two playthroughs. The main story is the same but choices in the side quests do affect how much more side quests (and achievements) to play through. Playing through more missions helps give you more credits to buy more programs and also to rank up your Hat reputation to unlock new programs and hardware. Missing out on reputation ranks does not seem to affect the main story, but it seems that the main story will not progress until you resolve the side quests (by finishing or rejecting them)

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
Midnight protocol plays more like a turn based board game with puzzles. You have two actions to move around the map, solve puzzles, break ICE (firewalls and traps), and maybe steal some money [strike] (I stole from a dead person's savings account saving up for their mom) [/strike], all while trying to complete the mission objectives. After every turn, the trace protocol will roll their dice and determine how much longer you can stay on the map until the trace bar completes. In later maps, there might be SysOps who will try to protect their network to try and stop you.

The turn based mechanic allows players to choose to play either fast and dangerous by rushing the objectives but might raise the trace quicker, or slow and stealthily by cloaking from the trace and slowly destroying hindrances but safely (better chance trace might not increase). Personally, I enjoy going through every nook and cranny so I take my time slowly stealthily going through the maps (didn't take Mask off most missions, even sysops). In my second playthrough, I found it wasn't all that necessary to play so slowly since most missions actually have enough trace bar to play quicker and more aggressively.

[h1] Story [/h1]
I thought the main story and even all the side stories were great. Side stories help build up the world, giving more information on the different organizations and how the world is. It also foreshadows themes really well back into the main story. Some side stories that aren't directly involved with the main story or the world, but these feel like easter eggs that reward players who enjoy looking through everything.

I don't write reviews very often but this game deserves one.   Midnight Protocol is an accessible hacker game where it really makes you feel like you are hacking without having to have all the technical know-how.    You input commands into a terminal (via keyboard, how novel!) but there are not so many as to feel overwhelming.  In fact a few basic commands are designed to make it as transparent as possible (such as 'deck' which will remind you what you have equipped).  Some programs also have options and a simple 'help' command will remind you how to input them.  The game really hits the sweetspot with accessibility and it also has nice ambiance and interesting story line.    

I enjoyed the variety of programs and deck hardware to choose from though i found some quite powerful, some quite situational, and some unnecessary but there is a lot of fun in figuring that out for yourself.   While early on i used the standard 'cloak' and 'dagger' everyone starts with, i evolved my strategy to use 'mask' which is powerful but slow but wound up enjoying using 'onion' the most.   Combine that with the hardware that gives a modest stealth boost and see what happens!   Takes some discipline though.

I also randomly and luckily equipped 'Ace' and 'King' in the hack where it is needed the most.  It made the hack a breeze but I couldn't think of needing these programs in any other hack.  As I said, quite situational.  But the game is quite forgiving and as long as you have a program or piece of hardware in your inventory, you can easily rollback the hack and re-equip what you need to start that hack over.  
The rollback feature may make the game even a little too easy but with that said, i found the game engaging and rare for me, something i concentrated on completing before i got distracted by my next game!   My main criticism of the game may be that, while i don't want to go into detail and spoil it, there were components of the plot i didn't like.  Let's just say it was controversial.   But overall the meaningful side quests and decisions that you make but come back to help or haunt you help make the overall experience quite fun.

I would highly recommend this to anyone interested in the hacking universe and good story telling (all revealed via email).  As I write this i even have to remember i have a mouse I can use and don't have to only use the keyboard!  Enjoy!
Neat game, it does feel a bit like the 1980s Neuromancer game (you can get 'warez and upgrade it and stuff. But also it's own game and I enjoy it.
